t: Lepanto was fought between rowing ships, the last major engagement in the Western world of that kind, and was in essence an infantry battle on floating platforms.
Both fleets depended on oarsmen who were largely enslaved, convicts or prisoners, and some of those freed from Ottoman galleys took up arms during the fighting.
The victory won no territory back: Venice accepted peace in March 1573 and ceded Cyprus, and the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within months.
dyk: Ali Pasha is supposed to have promised his Christian galley slaves their liberty if he won, while on the Holy League side the galley slaves were freed from their chains before the fighting began.
ev: Nicosia and other Venetian possessions on Cyprus fall to the Ottomans
Famagusta surrenders on 1 August, and the pope's blessed banner reaches Naples on 14 August
The Holy League fleet leaves Messina on 15 and 16 September, then learns that the Ottomans have moved to Lepanto
On 7 October the fleets meet in the Gulf of Patras and the fighting begins around noon
Pope Pius V dies and the League begins to unravel
Occhiali sails with 200 newly built ships and skirmishes with Colonna's fleet
Venice makes peace with the Ottomans on 7 March, ending the War of Cyprus and the Holy League

f.place: The Gulf of Patras, off the Greek coast near Lepanto (ancient Naupactus, Turkish İnebahtı), in present-day Greece
f.sides: The Holy League, led by Spain and Venice, under John of Austria: 206 galleys and six galleasses, with about 30,000 fighting troops and 40,000 sailors and oarsmen. The Ottoman Empire under Ali Pasha: 211 galleys and 63 galliots, with about 37,000 to 41,000 oarsmen, virtually all of them slaves, and up to 34,000 soldiers.
f.outcome: The Holy League captured 117 Ottoman galleys and sank or destroyed some 83 others. Losses were about 7,500 dead for the Christians and about 30,000 for the Ottomans, though other sources give 10,000 and 40,000.
